en: In the section "Discourse on the Four *Siddhāntas* Based on the Five Turbidities" composed by the Tiantai śramaṇa Zhànruán of the Tang Dynasty, regarding the correspondence between the kalpa and life-span and the world:
the kalpa and life-span are simply the two retributions—the dependent and the primary—which constitute the world. Sentient beings are those for whom [the teaching] is intended.
A person who perceives this and is able to calculate the perceiver is the same as ordinary sentient beings.
Because of these two, there arises the faculty of intentional action; thus, seeing ceases and goodness is born.

Afflictions (*kleśa*) are that which are to be countered; as in the five meditations for cessation (*pañca-vyupaśama*), they fully counteract the three poisons, and the correct application of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) can counteract turbidity; therefore, it belongs to the third category.
Furthermore, according to the intent of the treatise, the "ultimate meaning" (paramārtha) is applied in contrast to the Mahāyāna gate.
These four *siddhi* gates collectively answer the question regarding whether the five turbidities obstruct the Great [Vehicle] but do not obstruct the Small [Vehicle].
Because the four *siddhāntas* (the fourfold teaching) cover many instances, they are placed at the beginning of the section on "Discrimination.
From the passage "If one discusses cause and effect" onwards, the five turbidities (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*) are further analyzed through numerous categories.

The first [section] is the gate of cause and effect. The second "cause" refers to afflictions (*kleśa*) and views (*dṛṣṭi*); the remaining three are the meaning of "effect," which includes both the basis (*āśraya*) and the supported (*adhiṣṭhita*).

Next, from "one person" (*eka-pudgala*) onwards is the gate of persons (*pudgala*) and phenomena (*dharma*): "person" refers to sentient beings, while "phenomena" refers to the other four [aggregates]. Because they are contrasted with "beings," they all constitute phenomena; these are all that which is conceptualized by living beings.
Regarding "the four dharmas," this refers to the gate of sequential timing; it should be stated as "the four dharmas simultaneously," but the text is abbreviated.
"Timing" (時) here refers to kalpas, while the remaining four belong to the dharmas. If one speaks in relation to time, birth also belongs to the dharmas.
"Second, the obstacle of retribution" begins the section on the three obstacles.
Regarding "the two retributions," these are sentient beings and life.
Regarding "the two afflictions," since views are also commonly designated as afflictions, they are included here.
Regarding the phrase "karma exists within it": because afflictions moisten karma and karma is able to summon retribution, it is said to be "within it.
The section beginning with "sentient beings" refers to the three gates of provisional designation (*trividha-prajñapti*) from the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.
"Knowable through mutual dependence" refers to kalpas, afflictions, and views. Kalpas are mutually dependent in terms of length;
afflictions are mutually dependent in terms of opposition and conformity; and views are mutually dependent in terms of existence and non-existence.

If discussed generally, each possesses its own three types of provisional designation (*prajñapti*); there is not a single instance among the two retributions—the primary body and the environment—that is not formed through these three provisional designations. However, for the sake of analytical distinction, they are explained separately here; therefore, they are addressed individually.

Regarding "sentient beings" (*sattva*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains this through the gate of the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*). Sentient beings are designated as such through a combination of factors; life-force (*jīvitendriya*) and so forth are all dharmas conceptually imputed as sentient beings.

Furthermore, there is that which is reckoned as a provisional name (prajñapti-nāma) corresponding to sentient beings; therefore, it is said that "the name applies to both places. A detailed explanation is fully provided in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* commentary.

Regarding the phrase "afflictions" (*kleśa*), this distinguishes between the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and the noble one (*ārya*). As for afflictions existing in the ordinary person, it is simply because all ordinary beings necessarily possess them.

However, while [the view of self] must exist only in the ordinary person, afflictions extend to the noble ones as well, such as in the case of noble ones who are still bound by fetters (*sakalabandhana*) or those on the path toward Arhatship (*arhattvapratipannaka*).
Regarding the statement "the three [periods] are common": when the kalpa is in decline, there are Buddhas; when the kalpa is increasing, there are only ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, during decline there are Buddhas, while during increase it is common for other noble ones (*ārya*) to appear.
Moreover, both the periods of increase and decline are common to both existence and non-existence, because the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ in this regard.
How could the purity and fullness of the Flower Treasury World (Huazang) await the reduction of the kalpa?
This is what is meant by its constant presence on Mount Lingyan.

The term "sentient beings" (zhongsheng) applies universally to both ordinary beings and sages; as for "life," there are differences between the life of retribution for ordinary beings and that of sages.

Regarding the phrase "short lifespan," this refers to the gate of long and short [lifespans]: because one is born repeatedly within a single kalpa, there is a distinction between long and short. This is explained in terms of humans and the gods of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) as they encounter the Buddha; however, if one discusses the first dhyāna, the lifespan is equal to the kalpa. From the second dhyāna upward, the kalpa is short while the lifespan is long; this may be understood by applying the same principle to the formless realms (ārūpyadhātu).

Regarding "the three types of long and short": afflictions (*kleśa*) are long when present in ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and short when present in noble ones (*ārya*). Various views (*dṛṣṭi*) are long when present in other ordinary persons and short when present in those of sharp faculties among non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); alternatively, they may be short when present in other ordinary persons and long when present in those of dull faculties among non-Buddhists. Furthermore, they may be short when small because they are severed in a single lifetime, or long when great because one retains the afflictions to moisten birth and enter the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, one sees that the exhaustion of the preceding [afflictions] is short, while the exhaustion of subsequent afflictions is long.
Now, to distinguish those who enter birth and death through turbidity is not itself called "turbidity"; this is spoken of by analogy with sentient beings.

Regarding the "kalpa" (劫), there is the gate of whether it is accompanied by or not accompanied by [the aggregates]. Life (*jīvitendriya*) is a factor dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-dharma*); it must be discussed in terms of length and brevity of time by being accompanied by the aggregates (*skandha*). As for the others, they all belong to the category of dharmas and are not unaccompanied by time; because they do not directly accompany [the aggregates], they reside solely within the dharmas.

Regarding "the kalpas pervading" the lower section, there are internal and external gates: great kalpas (mahākalpa) are called "external" because they destroy the receptacle world (bhājanaloka), while small kalpas (antarakalpa) are called "internal" because they harm sentient beings;
alternatively, during the periods when the four turbidities (caturkaṣāya) gather, they pervade both the internal and external.

Regarding the "Three Small" [kalpas] under the section on Harm and Non-harm: the "objects" refer to the external receptacle world. When the great kalpa begins to arise, humans are reborn above; according to the three differences [of their karma], they are reborn in the three dhyāna realms.

Regarding the "minor kalpas" (*antarakalpa*), the gates of the five destinies and the three realms should properly be discussed separately; however, because the three and the five intersect with one another, they are explained here together. The general characteristics of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are as previously stated.

Regarding the term "supernormal power of life" (*āyur-abhijñā*), one should also state that the other four supernormal powers pertain to the three realms and five destinies; the details of the supernormal power of life are as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*.

Regarding the distinct lifespans across the five realms, such as the fifty years of human life and so forth, it should also be stated that these apply to all four modes of birth (*yoni*), for each of the four modes has its own varying duration.
The section beginning with "The *kalpa* is... constitutes the section on common and specific [classifications].
Next, from "Small Kalpa" onwards is the section on the general and specific gates.
From "From eighty thousand [years]" onwards, the large and small kalpas are explained.

Regarding the phrase "the three poisons being rectified," this refers to pure lands in other directions such as Akṣobhya’s land, where although there are women, they possess no lustful desires; thus, by citing one case, the others may be understood by analogy. Since the distinctions vary extensively across various lands, the note says "and so forth."

"Thoroughly true" (*dunzhen*) refers to those who have attained the genuine reality; thus, it excludes those who speak falsely, as well as those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), for there are ultimately none who do not believe despite lacking actual attainment.
"Succession" (*si*) likewise means continuity.

Regarding the phrase "the bodies are also immeasurable": in the teachings of the Hīnayāna, it is not said that there are further places of birth outside the realms; however, some reckon that the *parināmika* (transformation) rebirth exists within the realms and thus also designates it as a place of birth.
Since, in the teachings of the Mahāyāna, such places of *parināmika* birth are numerous, it is therefore described as "immeasurable."
This passage expresses a hidden intention; although the words merely state "called overweening pride," they actually refer to Arhats.
If one has truly attained this [state], how could there be anyone who does not resolve to attain the Great Mind?
He then refutes [the opponent] by means of the Mahāyāna in a cryptic manner.
If it is claimed that [the transformation] must ultimately be exhausted, then why do you not believe it if it has not yet been exhausted?
Regarding the phrase "encountering other Buddhas," the initial text refers to the Buddhas of the *sopadhiśeṣa* (with-remainder) lands as "other Buddhas."
Regarding the statement "Arhats receive bodies from previous lives": they are called "bodies from previous lives" because they are retributions for past karma.
Since they are the fruit of afflictions (*kleśa*), they must necessarily be extinguished.

If one were not extinguished despite being deluded by afflictions, there would be the fault of a discrepancy between cause and effect. Even if it were claimed that the power of the ultimate meditative concentration (*prāntakoṭi-samādhi*) sustains them so they do not perish, we now ask: is this ultimate concentration great or small?
If one speaks of it as "small," then being small, it lacks the designation of "change" and likewise lacks the doctrine of "eternal permanence.

If one speaks of it as "great," then at the limit of greatness, the name is set aside and it exists only as Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi); how could it be that immediately after receiving the prediction, one becomes Equal Enlightenment?

If it were the case that the great enters the small meditative absorption to manifest that the great has no fixed function, this would be incorrect—especially regarding those such as Rāhula cited [as examples].

This is because after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, various arhats manifested different modes of appearance and disappearance according to the specific conditions of sentient beings; how much more so for those who were originally great bodhisattvas?
This is because the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, in the *Mahāśāstra*, provisionally poses this question with the intention of having it answered exhaustively according to the Great Vehicle.
Thus, the response in the text states, "They do not arise within the three realms," and furthermore, the treatise itself cites the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to corroborate this.
Thus we know that the words of the common masses lack authoritative teachings to serve as a standard, and the doctrines of other lands originate from others.
Therefore, the ancients said:
"If one does not take [the sages] as teachers, learning will not be secure; if one does not find the Way within oneself, righteousness will not withstand difficulties."
Therefore, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is not indistinct on this point.

Furthermore, if the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) did not transcend the realm of existence, then such statements as "being born into the five destinies," the discourse on "re-entering birth-and-death," and the parable of "frighteningly entering the burning house" would not be texts concerning the single day of nirvāṇa, but would instead be mere fabrications.
Regarding the three explanations following "Nanyue," all are the interpretations of Nanyue.

In the subsequent explanation, it says, "If an Arhat practices the Buddha-remembrance samādhi," and so forth; if one speaks of remembering the Buddhas of the ten directions, this implies that they have already awakened the Great Mind (bodhicitta). If one remembers only Śākyamuni Buddha, it is because a small cause elicits a great response; this is likewise due to the awakening of the spiritual capacity (the *ki*).

However, within the Hīnayāna, the various schools differ; there are also those who believe in the Buddhas of the ten directions. Specifically, when followers of the Hīnayāna cultivate the power of concentration at the limit of the fourth dhyāna, they perceive the Buddhas of the ten directions and so forth; through the perfection of their mindfulness of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) contemplation, they are moved by the Buddhas to preach the Dharma for them.
Regarding the third point, the mention of "ordinary persons" (pṛthagjana) is intended to use them as a foil for the noble ones (ārya).
Therefore, it is logically impossible that an Arhat would fail to hear [the teaching].
Master Yao’s intention was as follows:
Among those who have truly attained arhatship, there are none who do not possess faith; for them, there is no need for another Buddha.
As for those who encounter another Buddha, these refer to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
How could Nanyue not know that ordinary beings can give rise to faith after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa?
Therefore, when encountering other Buddhas, they invariably point to the Arhat.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"Ordinary persons possess the capacity for regression and recovery, whereas Śrāvakas do not."
Thus we know that Śrāvakas are difficult to turn back and require consultation, whereas ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*) are easily influenced; why then need one cite examples [of the former]?
Regarding the passage from "Someone says" to "inevitably," the intent is to refute Master Yao; the argument established by one who does not believe is likewise incorrect.
The firmness of their adherence must surely lie in the ancient teachings; they should not rely on texts concerning the period after his parinirvāṇa as proof.

This master further cites the passage from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* where Śāriputra first hears the brief opening [of the Dharma] to prove the statement that Arhats do not receive [the prediction] after his parinirvāṇa.
The intention is this:

even when encountering a Buddha or an Arhat, one might still suspect them of being a demon; how much more so after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—how could one possibly be willing to believe and accept [the teachings]?
Now, however, it is not so.

Since the Buddha personally exhorted and urged them, there were none who did not believe; therefore, it is permissible for the provisional teachings recorded in the scriptures after his parinirvāṇa to be interpreted in such a manner.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth," one should extensively clarify the intentions behind the faith—or lack thereof—of both Arhats and ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) in order to refute this master as well as Master Yao.
The nine characters "This is merely a divergent interpretation" and so forth should perhaps be written in white ink;
this indicates that while the two preceding masters were not entirely mistaken, they simply did not fully accord with the intent of the sūtra.
Because it cannot completely refute [the opponent's view], it is called a "dissenting interpretation.

As for Master Yao’s view, which contradicts the scriptural text: the Sūtra states, "An Arhat encounters another Buddha and gives rise to faith, yet says it is not necessary," and the intent of this passage is that "except after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa" is intended to manifest the universal efficacy of the four reliances throughout the sūtras.

Yet, Yao does not regard the four reliances as "other Buddhas"; he claims that whether an Arhat’s three faculties hear [the teaching] or do not hear it, they never depend on hearing from the four reliances. This is profoundly untenable.
Furthermore, as for using ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) as an analogy, that would indeed be acceptable;
however, one must simply say they have "encountered the four reliances" (*catur-apāśraya*).
The later master’s intention is as follows:
"It is easy for ordinary beings, but difficult for arhats.
This also contradicts the definitive words of the sutras; therefore, it is said, "This meaning should not be employed.
Next, the verse is explained.

Regarding the statement that "the three or four groups, such as those with overweening pride (*adhimāna*), have these [faults] in common": furthermore, there are five different types of overweening pride among ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), namely those belonging to the four stages of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and the four fruits of the path (*phala*). While the general meaning is easy to understand, it will be explained separately later; however, because this is based on the majority of cases, the Sūtra states: "The four groups, beginning with the bhikṣus, possess these three faults. Within the specific distinctions of these three, it is still spoken from the perspective of those who clear away the mats; thus, it is so stated.
The phrase "concealing flaws" and so forth explains the three faults.

"Concealing flaws while extolling one's virtues" explains overweening pride (*adhimāna*); "being unable to reflect upon oneself" explains self-conceit (*asmimāna*); and "the shameless person" explains lack of faith (*aśraddhā*). If one perceives one's own faults, these three faults do not exist; thus, even if one has not yet realized the fruits [of the path], one is said to possess a sense of shame (*hrī*).

Regarding the phrase "in regard to the precepts" (*śīla*) and so forth: the term "precepts" refers generally to the ten types—namely, those described in the *Mahā-śāstra* and the *Mahā-sūtra* as being "neither deficient nor broken," and so on. Since it is verified that even the three types of transgressions do not constitute deficiency, how much less would the "path-concomitant" (*mārga-sahagata*) precepts? Therefore, the text speaks of "deficiency" and so forth.
There are three aspects of ethical discipline (*saṃvara*): namely, being unimpaired (*akhaṇḍa*), unpierced (*achidra*), and unbroken (*abhinna*), as well as being unmixed (*asamala*).

According to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, "unimpaired" refers to the third [aspect]; according to the *Mahā-sūtra*, "unimpaired" stands at the beginning. Although the names are identical, their meanings differ, each having its own intended significance, as fully explained in the *Vyākhyā*.

For now, following the *Mahā-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, we shall take the three types beginning with "unbroken" (*akhaṇḍa*), together with those associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi-samvara*) and those associated with the Path (*mārga-samvara*), to constitute the six precepts.

Thus, one should know that if the latter two among these six were absent, they would still be termed "outflows" (*āsrava*); how much more so when those associated with the Path and concentration are categorized within the Three Baskets and the Four Fruits of the Śrāvaka. For the time being, we shall discuss them in proximity to those that lack the Path and concentration.
Therefore, those who possess these three faults do not even have the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata), much less the four fruits of the path.

"Xia" (瑕) refers to an internal flaw in jade, hence it is called "arising within"; "ci" (玼) refers to an external flaw in jade, hence it is called "moving externally. External flaws are termed "defects" (khaṇḍa), while internal flaws are termed "leaks" (āsrava).

Regarding "smaller within the small": the four fruits [of the śramaṇa] are already small; the four dhyānas are even smaller; and wisdom is already extremely small—how much more so when combined with overweening pride (*māna*).

Regarding "dregs and husks": if one relies on worldly dhyāna to attain the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state, it is like dregs producing wine; entering the principle from the letter is like husks yielding rice.

Having already lacked the untainted state (anāsrava), they instead falsely calculate worldly dhyānas; this is like discarding the wine while retaining the dregs. Failing to attain the True Principle, they instead cling to words and letters; this is like discarding the rice while retaining the husks.
Regarding the phrase "these five thousand [people] exist," it uses existence to manifest that there is neither loss nor gain.
As for the term "clinging to the text," one should further say they cling to dhyāna as real, like dregs without wine.
Regarding the two interpretations in the text, the first is the correct one; the latter interpretation, however, also includes those śrāvakas who practice according to the letter.
Those who have merely "arisen" and "departed" likewise lack the great capacity for awakening in the present, and thus withdraw, being like dregs and husks without wine or grain.
"Branches and leaves" refers to those who lack the material for entering the Path.
Question: What is the distinction between "vessels" (the prepared) and these?

Answer: Although these are all based on metaphors, each carries its own specific meaning. "Capable of being inspired" refers to the potential for awakening (*indriya*), while "fit to receive the teaching" refers to the vessel (*bhājana*).

One who possesses a human or celestial body is generally termed a "vessel"; however, because they harbor the three faults, their status as a vessel is rendered invalid. Furthermore, since their past seeds are too faint, there is no potential for awakening to be aroused. Lacking both of these meanings, the Buddha’s majestic power causes them to depart.
Regarding the phrase "there are three differences," first they are listed and then explained.

First, concerning the statement "above there is a praise of the rarity of the Dharma": among the six sections of the preceding Chapter on the Buddhas, only the final two are absent; thus, there is a praise of the Dharma. The text says:

"Such a wondrous Dharma as this is preached by the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, only at certain times," yet it lacks the passage concerning the five turbidities (pañcakaṣāya). Furthermore, within the verse, there is no praise of the Dharma.
Regarding "prior and subsequent": the preceding section first praised the Dharma as cited above.
As for the term "not false," the subsequent text states:

"You all should believe what the Buddha has spoken; his words are not false. Furthermore, regarding the opening and clarification that joins the aforementioned exhortation to believe with the quality of being "not false," the preceding text says:
"You all should believe that what the Buddha has spoken is not false.

Regarding the phrase "now separated from what is not false," in this verse, the exhortation to believe comes first and "not false" follows later; they are separated by the passage concerning the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
Thus, there were four previously and five now, because the exhortation and the inspiration of faith have been treated as two.
It should be said that within the section on the non-falsity of the exhortation and inspiration of faith, there is an interval created by the five turbidities. Master Zhangan further states:

"Regarding the previous explanation that Śākyamuni’s skillful means are employed to explain the provisional teachings bestowed by all Buddhas—the preceding explanation of the Buddhas’ opening of the provisional was stated in the text: 'By means of countless skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and verbal expressions, I expound all dharmas,' as is seen in the verse."

Regarding the phrase "attaining all provisional dharmas through the cultivation of the path": this refers to the provisional dharmas manifested by the fulfillment of the causes of one's own practice; it is precisely the provisional [dharmas] within the substance of one's own practice.

This very essence of the Dharma is likewise ineffable; yet, through skillful means, it is taught for the sake of sentient beings to accomplish the provisional power of transforming others. This refers to the passage beginning with "illuminating the nine realms" and below. Thus, we know that the statement regarding "establishing the One and opening the provisional" now constitutes two meanings:
first, to restate the previous application of provisional means; second, to serve as the locus for revealing the ultimate reality.

If one does not point to that which is revealed, there is no way to speak of the ultimate reality; how much less so when pointing to the provisional as being provisional, thereby knowing it is not the final goal?

Once the ultimate reality has been manifested, the provisional is entirely seen as the ultimate. Regarding the phrase "illuminating the capacities of the nine realms to teach the seven expedients": the "nine" refers to those who are to be converted, while the teaching itself does not exceed the "seven. By teaching the seven to reach the nine, one gradually leads them into the ultimate reality. Because both persons and dharmas are categorized as either seven or nine, these collective terms are established.
The nine realms (dhātus) receive their names based on their own distinct characteristics, while the skillful means (upāya) are designated according to the process of advancement.
Furthermore, the nine realms are named after the capacities of sentient beings, whereas the skillful means are named after the transforming teacher.
To summarize the differences, it is said "seven and nine.
Regarding the phrase "cannot be definitively determined," this refers to which [type of] capacity among those seven or nine [beings] is involved,
and what teaching they hear.
Because they encounter opportunities according to circumstances, they are said to be "indeterminate.

Regarding the phrase "manifesting," since mindfulness must necessarily engage an object, it is called "manifesting"; the expression "various kinds" does not exceed the seven or nine [types of consciousness].
The section below on "the past" explains the nature of desire (*chanda*).
Since desire is nothing other than mindfulness (*smṛti*), we know that it was first explained as "longing" (*abhilāṣa*) and subsequently explained as "rejoicing" (*abhinandana*).

Therefore, we know that "recollection" (*smṛti*) refers to internal mental discourse, whereas "perception" (*saṃjñā*) arises in relation to external objects. Here, however, since we are dealing with the general category of desire (*kāma*) as it pertains to longing and attachment, there is no need to distinguish it by contrasting it with recollection; thus, it is simply categorized according to its nature across the two time periods [past and future].
Question:
Previously it was stated that the past is called the "root" (*mūla*) and the future is called the "nature" (*prakṛti*); why is it now said that the past is called the "nature"? Answer:
Each has its own specific meaning.

Since the nature (svabhāva) is necessarily unchanging, it is designated by the term "nature" both in the present and future, as well as from the past up to the present; thus it is so called because it receives the name of "nature" in these two positions.

Furthermore, it may be said that a faculty (*indriya*) arises in the future from the present; however, while the nature of the faculties can be cited interchangeably, the inclination (*chanda*) must reside in the present. Although the name "inclination" does not derive from the past, it can still be understood in relation to the future by means of the present, because the names are used interchangeably. Therefore, he explains again: "Either one cultivates inclination to form a nature, or a nature is formed which gives rise to cultivated inclination. In the former phrase, present inclination forms a future nature; in the latter phrase, a past nature forms present inclination.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth": it may be that one intends to establish the past as being present, or intends to establish the present as being future; or it may be that one intends to establish the past as being past, or intends to establish the present as being future. Thus, although the term "intention" (chanda) transcends the past and future, it is still spoken of in terms of the present. Therefore, we know that the designation "intention" is firmly established in the present.

Regarding the passage from "The Seven Expedient Means" to "and so forth," it is as fully explained in the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) under the section on "Contemplating Evil according to One’s Own Intent," where it speaks of "good and evil in their general application."
From "those of dull faculties" down to "the intention of employing skillful means," this constitutes the long prose section.

We do not refer to it here as "long" because the verses differ from the prose; rather, we shall distinguish their similarities and differences according to the essential points of each matter, or perhaps a brief clarification of the intent will suffice for understanding.

Regarding the principle [expounded] in the three verses beginning with "I have established," although the text frequently uses the term "teaching" (*vāda*), why is it here termed "principle" (*yukti*)?

This is because, as in expressions such as "never before taught" or "the time for teaching has not yet arrived," these [terms] likewise reveal the underlying principle through their capacity to manifest it.
Based on the preceding examples, this can be roughly understood; the present text specifically takes the Buddha’s wisdom as the practice of principle (*li*).
Regarding the phrase "Śrāvakas also include Pratyekabuddhas," it is because among the ranks of Śrāvakas there are those who encounter a Buddha and attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha.

Furthermore, since the Śrāvakas of the Tripiṭaka must also include those of the Pratyekabuddha teachings, and since Bodhisattvas already encompass both the Tripiṭaka and the Shared Teachings, the Two Vehicles must necessarily possess both types of teaching. As for why Bodhisattvas are not mentioned as being "distinct," it is because the distinct teaching was already concluded previously with the pure mind.

Since it has been established as a principle that both śrāvakas and bodhisattvas together shall all attain buddhahood even from a single phrase, and since he further cautioned them not to harbor doubts, one should know that this is the sincere teaching of the Ultimate Sage; yet they are unwilling to believe it.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"All followers of the two vehicles will in the future certainly return to the Great Parinirvāṇa, like water flowing into the ocean.
Furthermore, since the Bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles are explained together, one should know that all three vehicles are ultimately subsumed within this convergence.
Regarding the phrase "reciting the three provisional teachings," it is because the three teachings are provisional designations (*prajñapti*).

Since the essence of the teaching is the single reality, the three are provisional; they are expedient means such as the Three Baskets (*tripiṭaka*) provisionally established for the sake of sentient beings. Now that the reality has been revealed, [the text] again mentions what was to be eliminated to demonstrate the Buddha’s wisdom—this refers precisely to those items listed in the preceding sentence.
Regarding the statement, "The 'non-duality' refers to the duality of the provisional and the perfect within the Shared Teaching," this is because the Shared [Teaching] subsumes both.

Since it lacks the Distinct Teaching, the remaining vehicles above are further cited here to provide this explanation. If one speaks in terms of the provisional, this refers generally to the three teachings; the mention of "the remainder" and "two or three" merely describes their mutual inclusion. Because all that remains is provisional, they can mutually include one another; where there is nothing remaining, there is no longer the name of "mutual inclusion," as it is purely one. This refers to the milk, the two types of cream, and the three flavors, at which point the text concludes.
The first one and a half lines cite the internal mind.
The Sūtra says:
"That which I formerly vowed, that is now fulfilled. Question:
Question: When the Buddha first made his vow, he pledged to deliver all sentient beings. Since there are still so many sentient beings remaining, how can his vow be considered fulfilled? Answer:
For the time being, speaking in general terms regarding a single kalpa, if sentient beings are merely enabled to enter the Buddha Vehicle, this is called the fulfillment of the vow.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"As I am, so are they; there is no difference.

Regarding the passage beginning with "If I encounter sentient beings," this clarifies that turbidity does not obstruct the Great [Vehicle]. "Encountering" means causing all to enter the Buddha-way; it is called "obstructing the Great" because those lacking wisdom do not accept it.

Regarding the term "sentient beings" (*sattva*), there are three explanations in the text: first, it is explained as being designated in relation to others; second, it is explained as being so called from its own establishment; and third, it is explained as being identical to its functional capacity.
I fear that the new translation’s use of the term "sentient beings" (sattva) would be overly broad; while it excludes insentient things, it fails to capture all three meanings [of the original].

Regarding the statement that among the ten types of birth and death, those of the Brahma realm have "few words": this is because in the various levels of the desire realm, speech is natural and abundant. Since all speech arises from vitarka and vicāra, the fact that they speak little indicates that vitarka and vicāra are diminished. Because their afflictions gradually thin out, it is said that their lives are "short."
"Square" means that, just as square objects are fixed in their movement or stillness, having died here, one is certain to be born in the heavens.
"Triangle": "corner" (角) signifies a gathering (聚).

That is to say, they consist of the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate; throughout the cycle of birth and death, these three are omnipresent. In various Vinaya and Abhidharma treatises, they are most often referred to by the collective term "horns.
As for the omission of an explanation regarding the "purple" (zi), it refers to the asuras.
Because there are many varieties—such as those among devas, pretas, and animals—they appear like the color of purple.
Furthermore, regarding saṃsāra, the *Dṛṣṭatattva-samādhi Sūtra* states:
"Coming from the hells, their voices are hoarse and hurried, and they tremble repeatedly; they dream of great fires, boiling cauldrons, and the like."

Those who come from the realm of animals are dark-witted, indolent, gluttonous, and timid by nature; they are stammering in speech, and their actions mostly resemble those of various insects and beasts.
Those who come from the realm of hungry ghosts have yellow hair, are constantly hungry, and are characterized by stinginess and greed.
The other destinies are to be inferred by analogy; the Sūtra explains this in detail at length.

Regarding the phrase "I know," the following section specifically clarifies the five corruptions (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*). Although the previous chapter outline stated that the specific clarification of the five corruptions obstructs the three [jewels], the five corruptions themselves cannot necessarily obstruct the three. Rather, they are called "obstructions" because they are the objects to be remedied by the three, and thus constitute the obstructions that are to be remedied. Therefore, it is said that they are "obstructions."
Furthermore, because there is turbidity, the three [stages] are absent; and because the three exist, turbidity is absent—thus it is merely called an "obstruction.
Regarding the phrase "receiving the subtle form of the embryo," the initial text applies this directly to the contemplation of the mind (guanxin); this is simply for the sake of convenience.

It merely states that "following the mind" is called "contemplating the mind," yet in reality, this still involves an explanation based on phenomena; for it is by means of this single, most subtle thought-moment that [the afflictions] are made to increase.

Next, from "Receiving Conception" (*garbhāvakrānti*) onwards, the entire section explains the matter in terms of concrete phenomena; a brief summary is as found in the fourth fascicle of the *Zhi guan* commentary, which cites the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra*.
Some have established a full chapter on "Receiving Conception," but this is not essential for the present purpose.

Now, my intention lies solely in clarifying the meaning of the five corruptions (pañcakaṣāya); it is necessary to employ provisional means, and merely listing their names is sufficient to clarify the intent of the corruptions. Why, then, laboriously compose extensive chapters here, leading those on the mistaken path to claim that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also explains the five corruptions no differently than the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, just as worldly people say:
"The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also explains the three vehicles."
The errors are as follows.
Regarding the phrase "the aggregate-body of reception" (*upādāna-skandha*), one might suspect it refers simply to the *Garbha-avakrānti-sūtra*.
Generally, there are thirty-eight weeks discussed in terms of growth; however, texts such as the *Abhidharmakośa* list only five stages, stating:
First is the kalala; from that, the arbuda is produced; from that, the peśī arises; from the peśī, the ghana arises; and next is the praśākhā.

Regarding the phrase "as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*," this refers to the twenty types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (personality view), such as the views of permanence (*śāśvata*) and so forth, as fully cited previously.

As for the term "long duration" (*dīrghakāla*) and so on, the present text contains both meanings, which is why the *kalpa* receives the name "turbid" (*kaṣāya*); whereas in the preceding initial passage there was only the second meaning, and the first meaning appears only in the subsequent analysis.
In the chapter on the Buddhas of the Past, the first two lines represent the three aspects of Right Giving (*samyak-dāna*), which is termed "Giving as the Opening.

The first line provides a brief verse summarizing the aforementioned three [aspects]. Within this text, the inclusion of both the principle (*li*) for instructing others and the practice (*xing*) possessed by the practitioner carries two meanings: first, a general inclusion; since the other three [perfections] are already present, how could the practice be absent?
Second, a specific inclusion; namely, the two characters "Buddha-path" (*fudao*) encompass them both—the goal being the principle and that which attains it being the practice.

The first one and a half lines provide a general summary across the five vehicles; therein, human practice is combined with the teaching. This is because since there is human practice, there must be that from which it is derived, which is precisely the teaching.

In this context, the seven expedient means (upāya) are termed "distinct expedients" because those who follow the Tripitaka are fundamentally different from those of the Mahāyāna gate; thus, they constitute a permanent distinction. Although these terms appear frequently in other texts, here they are all designated as "distinct" because they have not yet attained identity with the Perfect [Teaching].

Regarding the two interpretations—advancing and retreating—within the Bodhisattva Vehicle presented in the following two lines starting with "If there be": there are likewise two meanings. The designation of the "Five Vehicles" applies only to the Deer Park; the name of the "Seven Expedient Means" extends through all three flavors [of the Tripitaka]; and the practice of the Six Perfections is not restricted to a single teaching and thus may extend through all three. Since the Tripitaka serves as the foundation, it is said that they concurrently encompass both the Shared and Distinct [teachings].

The passage beginning with "What is it? explains the characteristics of the practices of the three teachings and six perfections. As for the practitioner who proceeds through the stages of "neither mark nor non-mark," this is because the simultaneous negation of both is precisely that which is to be realized.
It should also emerge sequentially from the aspects of the three truths; however, when discussing them together as both with and without marks, they are simply the three truths.

Furthermore, once one has entered the stages (*bhūmi*), there is no further discussion of their differentiation; yet, within the Bodhisattva vehicle, it is said that "having previously heard the teaching, one has already achieved the unification of the teaching. If the Bodhisattva does not differentiate [the stages], why would it be necessary to cite the past to achieve the unification of the teaching?
Therefore, whenever the phrase "in the past" (*atīta*) is used, it always possesses two meanings:
first, that which was heard [by the Buddha] in the past; second, that which was already opened [to others] in the past.

Here, we are specifically speaking of what was heard in the past. As for "those who were already opened having all attained the Buddha-way," the former meaning accords with the explanation of the *vyavasthāna* (the ritual of transformation), while the latter meaning accords with the explanation of the completion of the opening. This applies to each and every vehicle in the sections that follow, and the same holds true for the Buddhas of the past.

In the section on the Two Vehicles, although there are instances of principle and practice, the fact that they do not mention the "combined teaching" is merely due to the brevity of the text; the preceding section on Bodhisattvas likewise uses three to encompass one.

Regarding the phrase "making offerings to the śarīra after the Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa": if one takes the present as a model for the past, it is as in the *Ekottarika Āgama*, where the Buddha, having personally lifted up the śarīra and praised it extensively, commanded that a stūpa be erected at the crossroads.
The Buddha said:
"Four types of persons should have stupas erected for them: a Wheel-turning King (cakravartin), an Arhat, a Pratyekabuddha, and a Tathāgata.
The latter section states:
The Wheel-Turning King has no grades; the Arhat has four grades; the Pratyekabuddha has five grades; and the Tathāgata has thirteen grades.
Ānanda asked the Buddha:
"For what reason is it so?"
The Buddha said:

"A Wheel-Turning King transforms others through his own conduct and constantly abides in the ten wholesome paths; an Arhat does not undergo further existence; a Pratyekabuddha attains self-awakening without a teacher; and a Tathāgata is fully endowed with all virtues."
If people of the world have not yet attained the first fruit of the path, how could they willingly settle for being equal to a Wheel-Turning King?
After his parinirvāṇa, they build stupas regardless of whether he has truly advanced or not; as soon as they move, they all reach three, five, seven, or nine stories.

Even if one follows the modern practice of constructing a square mound, the eaves still form a single tier; though this may seem obscure, is it not nonetheless a dark conflation with the first fruit of the path?

As for those who claim that stupas were built at the sides of square mounds, their interpretation is again mistaken; it causes the ignorant to worship only my own teacher, or even to pay homage to the lowly while facing the high. Furthermore, since such proximity would fail to establish the distinction between the honorable and the humble, the resulting inconveniences cannot be fully discussed. At best, this benefits the deceased in their dark realm, while leaving the living in their mundane obscurity.

Moreover, the term "śarīra" (relic) is now restricted to the Buddha; while the merit of making offerings to the Buddha’s śarīra belongs to humans and devas, it is only by opening up the causes from long ago that one may call it the "Buddha-way.
Furthermore, since it is difficult for those of ordinary substance to generate merit in the present age, the virtuous should follow this path rather than conforming to worldly customs.

Regarding the statement, "The master of the stages (bhūmi) says it is the stage of the youthful (kumāra-bhūmi)": as for why this stage is established with the name 'youthful,' ancient masters have said that the 'dwelling' (vihāra) is the agent who dwells, while the 'stage' is the basis upon which one dwells; thus, the name of the dwelling is applied to the stage. To name it from the perspective of the dwelling would already be too remote, so because its meaning is profound, the term 'stage' is added to it. Therefore, when the text below [the passage] criticizes it by saying it "deviates from the text," it is because the text itself only mentions the 'youthful one' (kumāra).

Regarding the phrase "vertically narrow": when one gathers minor good deeds horizontally to form the cause for Buddhahood vertically, then there is no contradiction between the horizontal and the vertical; it is neither deep nor shallow, yet it is both deep and shallow.

If one interprets "childlike purity" (tóngzhēn) as referring solely to the vertical dimension and excludes the horizontal, this is problematic; for not only does such a vertical depth lack correspondence with reality, but it also abandons the breadth of the text and contradicts its literal meaning. Thus, we know that both the narrowness of the vertical and the exclusion of the horizontal are flawed.

From "Ascending the Stages" (*dengdi*) downward, [the text] first refutes the error of regarding [the teaching] as merely profound, while still briefly setting aside the fault of regarding it as merely horizontal.

From "Now, by... onward is the formal explanation: by subsuming the "childish and the pheasant," it reveals the horizontal breadth; by pointing to the "subtle" (*wei*) as being "manifest attachment" (*zhu*), it distinguishes the vertical depth. Manifest attachment resides within the subtle; thus, what is profound is not truly profound, and what is subtle is not truly shallow. Pointing to the subtle as manifest attachment establishes the meaning of the "conditioning cause" (*yuanyin*); the contemplation of manifest attachment cannot be distinguished by this alone—the subsequent sections follow this same pattern.
Therefore, entering the stages to attain Buddhahood is like an asura crossing the ocean; this is based on the *Ratnakūṭa-alaṃkāra-sūtra*, which is why it says "entering the stages.
For an ordinary person, even a single hair’s breadth of goodness becomes a direct cause for attaining Buddhahood, like a person crossing the great ocean.
From "The Buddha is clear" (*buddha-vibhakta*) onwards, he re-establishes the reasoning to refute the two errors.
From "If it were as... onwards, he reiterates the errors to refute them.
Furthermore, drawing parallels between the preceding and following sections is also termed "contradicting the text."
If one fears that the matter of a youth is too trivial to correspond to the Buddha-way, how could a single chant uttered with a distracted mind possibly dissolve such doubts?

Since even joining the palms and raising the hands are all reasonable expositions, we know that it is merely a case of esteeming the Buddha-way while failing to recognize the opening of provisional means (*upāya*).
Regarding the phrase "hardly including the two vehicles": "hardly" (dài) means "almost" (jǐ).
It means "nearly.
One should rather say "not including them at all"; why is it merely "almost"?
"If one is still at the stage of the Youthful (kumārabhūta), one does not even encompass the six stages, let alone the Lesser Vehicle.

The section beginning with "Discussing the Profundity" concludes [the discussion on] their vertical narrowness; the section beginning with "The Samādhi is Vast" concludes the fault of such vertical narrowness.

Next, regarding the question and answer, the meaning of the response concerning the "three Buddha-natures" is as follows: That which was fashioned by past subtle roots of goodness, vows, and wisdom all tend toward Bodhi; just as the nature of fire is to move toward the sky and its logic is that it must eventually be extinguished, and the nature of water is to flow toward the sea and ceaselessly proceed, [the seeds] would have naturally reached fruition were it not for being obstructed by the fact that the power of vows and wisdom had not yet been applied. Therefore, they await the present opening [of the Dharma] to serve as the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditioning cause). If one considers the underlying intent of the transformation [of beings], why wait for this opening?

If one were to follow common sentiments and establish [the doctrine] based on superficial designations, yet now opens up the fundamental reality of the Dharma-realm by adhering to the immediate truth—how could this be constrained by common sentiments or limited by those flickering flames?

Although the region of Guanzhong established that "goodness does not receive retribution," they did not clarify that the essence of goodness is fundamentally integrated. Since sentient beings have, from time immemorial, been nothing but a flowing deluded self, whatever they cultivate has never occurred without being accompanied by it; from whom, then, would the statement "not receiving retribution" be established?
If we consider those who have already resolved their minds, this is induced by their vows and practices; how could it have anything to do with wholesome karma that is not received?
Prior to resolving their minds, they receive blessings according to their births—how could such wholesome karma be prohibited from being received?

Therefore, one should know that the statement regarding "non-reception" [of past vows] implies that the substance of goodness lacks power; it should be understood that while the causes for those [vows] already repaid have ceased, not even a hair’s breadth of goodness from those not yet repaid is lost. If one has previously aroused the mind [for enlightenment], it is like water deposited in the ocean; whereas repaying a limited cause is like a fruit ripening from a flower. Thus, regarding those causes not yet repaid, one should open up their restricted sentiments and those who have previously inclined toward the provisional vehicle, leading them through the path of the essence of the One Real Observation and the Great Vow. If it were otherwise, and one merely spoke of "opening" [the gates] without observation, then since the substance of goodness would naturally reach Bodhi, why would it be necessary to further cultivate the practices and vows for Bodhi?
Question:

If that is so, why does the original treatise state that "playing with sand as a child" and so forth—meaning the roots of goodness performed by those who have resolved upon bodhicitta and practice the path of a bodhisattva—are capable of realizing enlightenment, whereas these cannot be attained by ordinary worldlings or by those śrāvakas of fixed destiny who have not yet resolved upon bodhicitta?

Answer: This is spoken from the perspective of provisional teaching and does not refer to the fundamental goodness [of their nature]. Therefore, one should know that for those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*) whose [wholesome roots] have not yet manifested in the present or future, even if they possess past wholesome roots as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is ultimately no principle by which they can achieve enlightenment on their own; hence it is said that they are "incapable of attaining it."

If it had not been opened, then what was previously accomplished would have been in error; now that it has been opened, what was previously accomplished becomes perfected. Thus we know that the essence of goodness is fundamentally wondrous and conforms to the mind of the practitioner; for this reason, when the mind is opened, all past virtues are fulfilled.
Next, the "Great Sūtra" below explains the reason for the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).
The thirty-two marks fully enumerate the four propositions. The old [commentary] states:
"Those who have severed their roots of goodness (*icchantika*) definitely lack the nature of goodness; they possess only the nature of evil objects and the five aggregates of evil."
Those with roots of goodness possess the nature of the cause and possess the correct cause, yet both lack the nature of the fruit.

Hexi says: "The icchantika possesses the nature of the evil aggregates, while the person of goodness possesses the nature of the good aggregates; both possess the indeterminate, and both lack [the fruit], as previously stated."

Xinghuang’s three interpretations: the first is based on the perspective of principle (*li*). Principle itself is neither good nor evil, yet it possesses those two functions; this refers to the fact that each of the two individuals has its own respective function of either good or evil.
Regarding "both existing and both non-existing," this is because they each possess one side of existence and non-existence in relation to one another.
The other two interpretations are unnecessary. Zhan’an said:

This explains the seven types of sentient beings within the river of nirvāṇa: it should be said that those who lack the aspiration for enlightenment (icchantikas) are constantly submerged, while virtuous persons are constantly emerging; those who possess both [the aspiration and its obstruction] remain together within the river, and those who lack both do not reach the shore—where "lacking both" refers to the absence of the nature of fruition as well.

Furthermore, explaining this in terms of the three truths: icchantikas possess only the causes of evil according to the worldly truth (saṃvṛti-satya); virtuous people possess only the causes of goodness according to the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya); both possess the resultant body according to the worldly truth; and both lack the causes and fruits of the Middle Way.

Although there are slight differences among the various Śākya traditions, the essential meaning of a single phrase from the virtuous ones is largely the same. As for those points where they differ, I lack the leisure to explain them here; they are fully detailed in the fifth commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*. Therefore, I shall now cite the points of agreement to corroborate the goodness of the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).
Question:

In the preceding explanation of the Three Vehicles, it was stated that the principle is established through the perfection of the fruit. Now, why is the Buddha-way taken as the contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) for the vehicles of humans and devas? Answer:

The revelations differ: previously, both the two vehicles of the two teachings as well as the common and distinct bodhisattvas were revealed to possess the principle of realization; therefore, the small principle was opened up to constitute the great principle.

Now, the minor wholesome deeds of humans and devas are revealed as having already become the "causal conditions" (*nidāna-hetu*) for great goodness; however, this is based on the fact that the essence of the goodness toward which they can tend has not yet deepened. If one speaks from the perspective of the goal toward which they tend, then these [deeds] all possess their respective resources. This treatise’s revelation of the provisional (*upāya*) is entirely based on the stages of the path; if one follows the process of actual entry, how could it be limited merely to the causal conditions prior to abiding in the stage of the "Dwelling" (*vihāra*)?

In this context, the explanation is given solely from the perspective of past events; since human affairs have already been settled, one cannot preserve the Dharma while discarding the person. Therefore, it is opened up as a contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*); is this not like a poor man finding a treasure?

Regarding the mention of the "seven treasures" and so forth in the Sūtra, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* does not include rose quartz; furthermore, it states that lapis lazuli (*vaidūrya*) and pearls are distinct substances, with "pearls" specifically referring to red pearls (*lohitamukti*).
Now, when combined with lapis lazuli, they constitute seven treasures; if separated, they become eight.
*Kācaka* (glass) is mostly red in color; *śaṅkhaśilā* (conch-shell stone) is bluish-white; and *musāragalva* (agate) is either white or blue.
Regarding "mukhā" (木櫁), the *Zilin* states:
"A cut [of] fragrant wood; the rhyme dictionary writes it as 榓. The *Yupian* states:
"The tree resembles the *huái* tree and is fragrant.
Someone said: "It takes five years of being cut before it begins to emit fragrance."

Regarding the phrase "creating images is a celestial task": it is as when the Buddha ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and, by means of his supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*), disciplined his disciples and others, as fully detailed in the first commentary of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Cessation and Contemplation).

According to the *Mingxiang ji* (Records of Miraculous Auspiciousness), there are a total of eighteen instances in this land where the creation of images resulted in miraculous responses, such as the stone image in the Wu region.

Furthermore, there was the image manifested by the daughter of Wu Pei, the Governor of Wuxing; and likewise, when Prince Lin Kang of the Song dynasty’s Guard Commandant was stationed in Jingzhou, he built a three-bay hall within the city walls with many painted Bodhisattva images on its walls. When Prince Wen of Hengyang succeeded him in governing Jiangling, the hall was converted into a dormitory and plastered over; yet when the plaster dried, it all peeled away, leaving the painted figures as fresh and clean as ever, without a single mark of defilement. Even after being replastered, the same occurred.
The king did not believe or respect this, regarding it as a mere coincidence; he then smeared the wall with thick mud, yet the image remained clearly visible.
The king again defaced the old wall and had it entirely renovated.
Later, when the King fell ill, whenever he closed his eyes, he would see various images filling his vision in dense profusion; it was only then that he ceased [the project] and resided here.

This may be because the creator’s mind was heavy with merit, or because the destroyer’s offense was particularly grave; by regarding the light as weighty and the destruction as an accomplishment, one should know that even a slight good deed performed with a distracted mind is not lost, for in principle there is neither opposition nor compliance, though the mind itself possesses right and wrong.

Regarding the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* and other such texts, the intended meaning here is precisely to elucidate their wholesome qualities without discussing their faults; it is only because the use of glue was mentioned that they were explained in this context.
Now, based on this and relying upon that [sūtra], I shall briefly clarify it; thus, that sūtra extensively explains the characteristics of upholding and violating the five precepts.
It further states:

"If one does not uphold the precepts, one is called a defiled upāsaka, a foul-smelling upāsaka, or a caṇḍāla upāsaka. If one upholds the precept against killing even toward an ant, or upholds the precept against alcohol even toward a drop of dew, and adds the prohibition against selling alcohol to these five precepts, these are known as the six grave prohibitions."

Now, those who have left the household life and those who remain at home claim to uphold the precept against alcohol, yet they still mix wine with their food; how many drops of dew does one person consume in total?
This is not even equal to the Upāsaka precepts—how can one expect to attain the Buddha-way?
Beyond the five precepts, there are numerous further offenses of losing one's mind; these are not fully detailed in the present text.

Furthermore, there are instances of losing one's mind, such as failing to make offerings to teachers and monks, failing to attend to the sick, pointlessly sending away beggars, not rising to welcome the fourfold assembly or senior elders, and seeing those who have broken the precepts and saying, "They are not as good as I."
Failing to observe the eight precepts on the six days of fasting; failing to attend a Dharma lecture within forty *li*;

accepting bedding, seats, or furniture belonging to the *saṃgha* or the *caitya*; drinking water while suspecting it contains insects; traveling alone through dangerous places; staying overnight alone in a nunnery;
beating one's own servants or others for the sake of wealth or life; and seeing [a person] on the road—

A bhikṣu or śrāmaṇera must not walk ahead [of their preceptor]. When food is being distributed among the Saṃgha, one must not give preferential treatment to one’s own preceptor or give them an excessive portion.
If one encounters someone who is ill while traveling on the road, one must not fail to attend to them or look after them, nor fail to entrust someone else to provide care.
One who upholds such precepts is called a pure, fragrant, and white-lotus (puṇḍarīka) upāsaka.

Furthermore, lay followers (upāsakas) are enjoined to provide various offerings to the images, stupas, and temples of the Triple Gem. When painting images, one must not use milk-glue or egg whites. When making offerings to an image, there should be no difference between day and night; one must not smear the body of the image with ghee or oil, nor wash it with milk. One must not create half-body images; if an image’s body is incomplete, it should be kept hidden.
One should encourage others to restore [the image]; once restored, one should provide offerings.

Furthermore, seeing a damaged image as no different from one that is entirely non-existent and offering the treasures of the four continents to it is not equal to directly praising the honored image with various merits and making offerings with a sincere heart; the two blessings are indistinguishable.

As for the method of making offerings, one should with a sincere heart of faith and joy accept, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe [the teachings], practicing according to the Dharma and encouraging others to do so. One should transcribe the twelve divisions of the scriptures in various ways and make offerings to them as one would to the Buddha; this is called the "method of making offerings," with the sole exception of bathing [the scriptures].

Regarding the making of offerings to the Sangha: one should offer to those who have resolved to attain bodhicitta, those who have left the household life to uphold the precepts, and those who have attained the four stages of progress and the four fruits of arhatship; this is called making offerings to the Sangha.
Now, even minor virtues in this sutra serve as causes for Buddhahood, let alone long-term offerings made with a sincere mind.

Although these belong to lay *upāsakas* and contain some elements that do not strictly accord with the formal intent of the text, they are established precepts (*pratikṣepa-śikṣāpada*) that one must observe; observing them constitutes the goodness of humans and devas and may all be opened up as contributory conditions (*nidāna-pratyaya*). Furthermore, they are essential for practitioners who have left the household life and are worthy of being adopted as a constant rule; therefore, I have recorded them here.

Now, this sutra intends to gather all subtle merits from time immemorial so that they may all lead toward Bodhi; if one has already resolved to attain enlightenment, then even a hair’s breadth of goodness serves as a contributory cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).

Regarding the precept in the *Śīla-sūtra* stating, "One must not sit before an image," and so forth, there are many other circumstances to consider, such as when facing dangers from kings or other perils, in which case one should exercise discretion according to the situation.
Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Merit of Image-Making* sets forth eleven merits: first, having clear and pure eyes in every lifetime;

second, being born in places free from evil; third, always being born into noble families; fourth, having a body the color of purple-polished gold; fifth, possessing an abundance of rare treasures; sixth, being born into families of the wise and virtuous; seventh, being born to become a king; eighth, becoming a Golden Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*); ninth, being born in the Brahma Heaven with a lifespan of one kalpa; tenth, not falling into the evil realms; and eleventh, being able to again revere and honor the Triple Gem in future lives.
One should know that how could these be the roots of goodness of humans and devas in the desire realm?
Regarding "lead" (*sīsa*) in the *Sūtra*, some say it refers to tin (*rīti*).
Now, it is said that lead is blue and tin is white; though lead is soft and tin is hard, both are termed "blue metal" (*nīlakaṃcana*). The *Sūtra on the Merit of Casting Images* states:

"If a person, at the moment of death, speaks of creating an image—even one as small as a grain of wheat—it can eliminate the sins of birth and death committed over eighty billion kalpas throughout the three periods of time."
"Temple" (miào) means appearance (mào).

The ancient term was "caitya" (zhīdì), while the new term is "caitya" (zhìduō); when translated as "spiritual temple," it should be written with the character miào. Both the *Yùpiān* and the *Báihūtōng* state that it is "the dwelling place of a venerable appearance."
Regarding the statement, "The dew-dish became a bronze cymbal," this sound did not exist in Chang’an either;
it may be that the pronunciation shifted, or perhaps someone at that time transmitted it, and Zhāng’ān simply recorded it as he heard it.
The *Sūtra* says that what is called "bai" (bhāṣya) is sometimes called "baini" (bhāṇaka);
this is translated as "chanting praise. This practice originally existed in the Western Regions.

According to the Liang dynasty’s *Xuanyan ji* (Records of Verified Manifestations), Prince Chen Si (Cao Zhi), styled Zijian, was the fourth son of Emperor Wu of Wei. At the age of ten, he was proficient in literature and the arts, and privately devised the rotation of the seven musical tones.

Zhi once traveled to Yushan, where, amidst the rocky valleys, he heard the sound of sutra recitation; its beauty resonated through the distant gorges, so he imitated it to create this specific mode of chanting.
This is exemplified by accounts such as those of the bell-ringing bhikṣu in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*.

Regarding "making offerings with music," when members of the monastic community have musical instruments accompanying them and speak of making offerings, one should reflect for oneself: with what state of mind is this being performed?

Although this text exists, it must be carefully scrutinized. Since the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* already strictly prohibits such acts, what need is there for further insistence? I fear that with a weak intention of making offerings, one might instead increase one's own negligence, foster greed and arrogance in others, and find it difficult to cultivate a mind of reverence. Thus, the fifth fascicle of the *Separate Translation of the Āgamas* records: "When the Buddha was in the city of Kalandaka, there was a courtesan named Dīrghakeśā who addressed the Buddha, saying:

'In the past, I heard from an elderly courtesan that by arranging various forms of amusement and laughter in a brothel to attract hundreds of thousands of spectators, such a person, upon the end of life, would be reborn in the Ābhāsvara Heaven. Is what she said false or true?'"
The Buddha told him:
"Stop, stop!
Do not ask such a question."
The host of courtesans questioned him again, repeating this three times.
The Buddha did not answer at all.
Then the Tathāgata spoke to the host of courtesans, saying:

At that time, hundreds of thousands of people came to see the performers; since these people were originally already entangled by the three poisons, would their greed, hatred, and delusion not increase further as they engaged in such acts of heedlessness?
It is like a person bound by a rope made of hair; if water is poured upon it, its tightness only increases.

Originally bound by the three poisons, if one further engages in music and entertainment, one will only cause the fires of the three poisons to blaze even more fiercely; that such a person should later be reborn in heaven is impossible.
"One who speaks such words is a person of wrong view; the fruit of wrong view is rebirth in hell.
When the Buddha said this, the courtesan’s master wept bitterly.
The Buddha said:
For this reason, he did not preach despite being requested three times.
The host of courtesans said:
"I do not grieve because I have not heard the Buddha's teaching; rather, I pity these courtesans who have been speaking in such a manner for a long night."

Some cite various sutras to this effect, stating that those who offer flowers, incense, and music as worship immediately attain non-retrogression, such as the *Avaivartika-dharmacakra-sūtra*, which says: "The Buddha told Ānanda:

'By offering even a single flower to the Buddha or a Buddhist stupa, one also attains non-retrogression,'" and the *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*, which states: "Through prostration, one reaches Great Nirvāṇa," and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "those [causes] have already become real causes," the present text clarifies that the coarse is itself the real; therefore, it does not conform to the previous case.
As for those who cite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding small causes and great fruits, the lack of conformity is likewise the same.

Regarding the phrase "May he deliver me to bestow [benefit] upon sentient beings": if one discusses the delivering of oneself, it should pertain to the capacities of others; "bestowing" (śi) refers to the establishment of a provision (*prajñapti*).

Now, because Śākyamuni, having heard the consoling words of the Buddhas of the ten directions, addressed the homage *namo* to those Buddhas, we know that Śākyamuni did not request the Buddhas to deliver him.

Regarding the passage from the "Sūtra on the Five Precepts" up to "offering to the Buddha," although it follows that the Buddha likewise has no reason for alarm or fear, according to the analogy below where the elder, having heard [the news], was startled and entered the burning house, it is logically appropriate that the Dharma-body experiences alarm and fear when contemplating the capacities of sentient beings.
Regarding the phrase "Joyfully proclaims: Namo Buddha," this explains "Namo" (homage) within the context of compliance.
As for the passage in the *Pañcaśīla-sūtra* concerning the explanation of "taking refuge" (*śaraṇa-gamana*), it says as follows: [and so forth].
Regarding the passage beginning with "The *Nāgasena-sūtra*," that sutra states:

"When Nāgasena was young, there was an old acquaintance who was the king of a small frontier state; he was skilled at posing difficult questions, and there were many exchanges of question and answer that also served to resolve minor doubts."
Nāgasena said:
"The śramaṇas say that the fire of the world is not as hot as the fire of hell.
The King asked:

If one places a small stone in a worldly fire and it does not melt until evening, yet a large stone placed in the fires of hell melts immediately, why does the evil person who has died and entered hell not melt after hundreds of thousands of millions of years?
Nāgasena asked:
"Do the fish and sea-monsters in the water feed on stones?
The King replied:
"So it is. Nāgasena asked:
"Does stone dissolve?"
The king said, "It has dissolved. Nāgasena asked,
"Does the child within your womb dissolve?"
The king said,
"It does not fit. Nāgasena said:
"Why does it not dissolve?
The king replied,
"It is due to my merit."
Nāgasena said:
"In the hells, because the evil karma has not yet been exhausted, it does not dissolve; it is like a wolf eating a bone—the bone dissolves, but the marrow does not.
He asked again:
Does the Buddha possess the marks and signs? Answer: He does.
The King asked:
"Does the Buddha have parents?
He replied:
"No. The King said: "The Buddha also has no [such distinction], for all people born resemble their parents."
Nāgasena said:
"Does the King see the lotus?
He replied: [Yes].
[The Buddha] saw him. He asked again:
"Was it born from mud?"
Answer: It was born from mud.
Nāgasena said:
"Is it because a lotus grows from mud that it resembles the mud?
The Buddha is also like this.
The King asked again:
"One person died and was reborn in Kaśmīra; another died and was reborn in niraya. Who arrives first? Nāgasena replied:
"It is like two birds flying together from there to here; one alights on a high tree, the other on a low tree. Of the two birds in flight, whose shadow reaches the ground first?"
The King said:
"They both reach the ground.
The King said:
"Excellent! Excellent!
Although the remaining text is not the primary intent of this commentary, it may be understood incidentally through it.
Furthermore, it increases wisdom and refutes heterodoxy to manifest the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection).
Regarding the *T’ai ching*, the *Pao-en ching*, and the "Hua-lin Assembly," the sutra states:

"In the first assembly, nine billion six hundred million people were delivered; in the second assembly, nine billion four hundred million people were delivered; in the third assembly, nine billion two hundred million people were delivered. These are all those who attained the fruits of realization through the Initial Teaching (*shikyō*).
"At that Buddha’s place, up until the fifth period, they were all likewise gathered in the assembly.

Regarding the phrase "if one follows the above," etc.: following the texts on the six *pāramitās* above, the three teachings were concluded as these three phrases; now, the wisdom of the *liǎoyīn* (cause of penetration) is also like this, for it opens up the partial and the small to establish the Real.

Furthermore, the expression "neither-nor" (ubhayābhāva) originated with the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka; it differs from that of ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle, and even for those on the stages prior to the Grounds of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*), this must be opened up. However, one must also know the reason why it is opened: if the mind is coarse while the object is subtle, one only opens the mind—as when one maintains the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* with a conceptualizing mind, or hears a single phrase or verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. If the object is coarse while the mind is subtle, the object has already followed along with the transformation of the mind, so there is no need to discuss opening it. If both are coarse, both mind and object must be opened; alternatively, one may simply open the mind, for there is nothing that will not undergo transformation. In principle, one must understand the essential nature of the good before it can be termed "opening."

In short, if both mind and environment are opened, even the long-standing coarse wisdom of the four evil realms can be opened, let alone the wisdom of humans and devas; for if they are not opened, the Buddha’s knowledge and vision will forever remain buried within the four evil realms, and one will remain submerged for a long time among humans and devas.

The intent behind these questions and answers is to open up the subtle roots of goodness from the past and directly strike at the mind’s present attachments. Having already been opened by the Buddhas of the past, those who hear even a single phrase of a sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and receive a prediction of enlightenment are cases where the depth of their realization is illustrated through the metaphor of their passing away; in both instances, their minds have been pre-opened so that both the subjective mind and its objects become sublime. Even for those who do not believe this sutra after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, it is still entrusted to them within the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to open their minds.
The intent of the Sūtra states explicitly that all three periods of time are opened [to the same teaching]; how could I not agree?

Regarding the statement, "The future Buddhas’ two-line verse is the teaching of one," since the Sūtra text says, "although it is taught" and "therefore it is taught," we know this refers to the oneness of the teaching.

Regarding the first line, the first three phrases—“although one speaks of hundreds of thousands of billions,” and so forth—refer to how all provisional teachings of the seven stages of preparation collectively constitute the cause for enlightenment; the phrase “in reality, for the sake of the Buddha-vehicle” clarifies the underlying intent behind these provisional teachings.
